title: ר' שמעון בן יוחאי

paragraphs: 2. He is the unspecified R' Shimon: Rashi, Shevuot 2b; Rashbam on Bava Batra 102a. Although the unspecified R' Shimon in Avot, chapter 2, who said “Be careful concerning the recitation of the Shema,” is R' Shimon ben Netanel: a matter learned from its context.

3. He was accustomed to miracles, in the matter of the cave. Rashi: therefore they sent him to annul the decree. As in Me'ilah 17a–b, he came from the Land of Israel to Rome with his colleague R' Elazar son of R' Yose ben Halafta and annulled the persecution. The demon Ben Temalyon entered the emperor's daughter's body, and R' Shimon ben Yohai expelled it. Tosafot there write that R' Shimon ben Yohai was irascible, easily angered, and exacting over a small matter. He cursed R' Elazar son of R' Yose. He said to him, “Remember that you vowed to my father not to punish me.” He prayed for him, and he recovered. One pupil went abroad and became wealthy. His pupils envied him and wanted to go abroad. R' Shimon ben Yohai knew through divine inspiration, took them to a valley, prayed, and said, “Valley, valley, fill with gold dinars.” So it was. He told them, “If you wish, take; but know that whoever takes now is taking his share of the world to come”: Rabbah, Pekudei, chapter 52. He saw someone gathering seventh-year aftergrowth and asked, “Is it not forbidden?” He answered, “Do you not permit it?” He said, “Do my colleagues not disagree with me?” He applied to him, “Whoever breaches a fence, a snake shall bite him,” and so it happened to him: Jerusalem Berakhot, first chapter, mishnah 2. He said, “I have seen those of ascent, and they are few … if there are two, my son and I are among them.” They can exempt the whole world from judgment; if Yotam son of Uzziyahu were with them, they could exempt it from the world's creation: Lulav va-Aravah, 75b [parallel at Sukkah 45b]. Arukh, entry Patar, writes that it became clear to R' Shimon ben Yohai that all the righteous had received in this world something of what is reserved for the world to come. These three—he, his son, and Yotam—had received nothing; therefore their merit is greater than that of other righteous people to protect their generation. Bereshit Rabbah, and Jerusalem Ha-Ro'eh, mention R' Shimon ben Yohai and Ahiyah the Shilonite; so too in Zohar. Perhaps he mentioned these because they greatly honored their fathers.

In Shabbat 33b, R' Yehudah began, “How fine are this nation's works! They established markets, bridges, and bathhouses.” R' Yose was silent. R' Shimon ben Yohai responded, “Everything they established was for their own needs ….” Yehudah ben Gerim went and related the matter, and it reached the king. He said, “Yehudah, who exalted, shall be exalted; Yose, who was silent, shall be exiled to Tzippori; Shimon, who disparaged, shall be killed.” He and his son R' Elazar went and hid in a cave. A miracle occurred: a carob tree was created for them—a miracle within a miracle, for it does not bear until seventy years, Hiddushei Aggadot—and a spring of water. They took off their garments and sat in sand up to their necks; at prayer time they dressed, covered themselves, and prayed. They sat twelve years. Eliyahu came, stood at the cave entrance, and said, “Who will inform bar Yohai that the emperor has died and the decree is annulled?” They came out and saw people plowing and sowing. He said, “They leave eternal life and engage in temporal life!” Wherever they directed their eyes was immediately burned. A heavenly voice went forth: “Have you come out to destroy My world? Return to your cave.” They went and sat another twelve months. A heavenly voice said, “Come out of the cave.” Wherever R' Elazar struck, R' Shimon healed, and so forth. R' Pinhas ben Yair, his son-in-law, heard—see his entry: he was his father-in-law; see there for what requires examination—and so forth. He said, “Woe to me that I see you so!” He answered, “Happy are you that you see me so ….” Originally, when R' Shimon ben Yohai raised an objection, R' Pinhas ben Yair would give twelve resolutions; afterward, when R' Pinhas ben Yair raised an objection, R' Shimon ben Yohai would give twenty-four resolutions, and so forth. He said, “I shall repair something ….”

In Bereshit Rabbah, Vayishlah, chapter 79, and Midrash Kohelet, at “Whoever digs a pit,” and Jerusalem Shevi'it 9:1, somewhat differently: there were places of doubtful impurity, and it troubled the priests to go around them. He cut up lupines; wherever a dead person lay, he rose to the surface. A Samaritan went and hid a dead person, then told R' Shimon ben Yohai that he had not purified that place. R' Shimon ben Yohai perceived through divine inspiration that he had hidden him there, and said, “I decree that the upper ones descend”—meaning that the Samaritan descend below—“and the lower ones”—meaning the dead person—“rise.” So it was.

4. The anonymous Sifrei is R' Shimon. Not as the author of Halikhot Olam writes at the end of gate 1, that it is R' Yishmael, and “all are according to R' Akiva,” his teacher. He erred, because R' Yishmael was not R' Akiva's pupil; see his entry. Yuhasin writes, in the order of the generations: likewise Sefer ha-Zohar, which illuminates the whole world, called Midrash Yehi Or, containing the Torah's secrets, was named after him, although he did not make it. His pupils, sons, and pupils' pupils made it from what they received from him, as we said that Mishnah, Sifra, Sifrei, and Tosefta are all according to R' Akiva, although these books were made on his authority more than sixty years after his death. That is, Sifra and so forth were made sixty years after R' Akiva's death; likewise Zohar was composed after R' Shimon ben Yohai's death by his pupils' pupils. But Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah, 31b, writes that if Zohar were complete it would be a camel-load, and it was composed about sixty years after his death. He understood Yuhasin's statement as saying that it was composed sixty years after R' Shimon ben Yohai's death. This is not so, for it says “these books were made,” in the plural, referring to Sifra, Sifrei, and Tosefta, which R' Akiva and his pupils made sixty years after his death. וק״ל [provisionally: this is readily understood]; see Novlot Hokhmah's lengthy discussion of this.

For this reason, Zohar's words are more true, because they are the words of later scholars, who saw the Mishnah, the halakhic rulings, and statements from the amoraim there. This book was revealed after Ramban and Rosh, who had not seen it. It is already agreed in Israel that where something does not contradict the Talmud, is not explicit in the Talmud, and we find it explicit there, we accept it. For example, Amen after Ga'al Yisrael: although Rashi, ר״ח [provisionally Rabbenu Hananel], Halakhot Gedolot, and Rabbenu Yaakov mentioned it, it is not found in Tosafot or Rambam; but in the rulings on Berakhot, Rosh's ruling in accordance with Rashi is found. Likewise, kiddush over wine at the third meal, which is not explicit in the Talmud: Rambam says it is required, although Rosh says it is not required, explaining that just as one kiddush suffices for the night, so for the day. This is a weak reason, because at night there is only one meal, whereas by day one is obligated in two meals. Zohar agrees with Rambam's view. Likewise, tefillin on the intermediate festival days: Raavad and Ramban did not prohibit them, apart from the author of Sefer ha-Mitzvot and Rosh. Since it is not explicit in our Babylonian Talmud, we take Zohar's opinion, that it is forbidden. Likewise, Grace after Meals by an individual: Rambam rules that it does not require a cup, whereas Rosh rules that it does require a cup. We find in Zohar that it requires a cup only with three, like the three patriarchs.

Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah, there, writes: I saw a puzzling thing in Yuhasin. Around the year 5050, groups of people arose who said that Zohar's words in the Jerusalem language are R' Shimon ben Yohai's, whereas those in the holy tongue are not his. Some say that Ramban found it in the Land of Israel and sent it to Catalonia; it went to Aragon and fell into R' Moshe de Leon's hands. Some say that R' Moshe de Leon was a sage who made these interpretations from his own understanding; to obtain a large price from the sages, he wrote them and attributed them to R' Shimon ben Yohai and his company, because he was poor and had many dependents. End of Yuhasin's quotation; see there at length. But I believe that it is all vanity, and the truth is that R' Shimon ben Yohai and his holy company said these things, and much more. It may be, however, that their words were not written in their generations in proper order, but in scattered booklets, and in the course of time were assembled properly, as our holy Rabbi did in composing the Mishnah and as Rav Ashi did in composing the Gemara. End of Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah's quotation.

5. He lived long after R' Yishmael: Tosafot, Yoma 59a. When he died, he saw R' Pinhas ben Yair and Rav Hamnuna the Elder coming to accompany him; they had died earlier. See their entries for what is very puzzling. See his death in Zohar, Ha'azinu, עתקע״ה [Heilprin’s locator; parallel at III 296b, Idra Zuta]. He was buried with his son R' Elazar in a cave; see his entry. גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael] writes: in Kefar Meron, R' Yohanan the Sandal-maker is buried. Close to him is an unroofed study hall, within which is a monument: R' Shimon ben Yohai is buried on the south side, his son R' Elazar on the west. Near the study hall entrance is Rav Adda the Elder's monument. At the place where one descends to the river is a cave: Hillel the Elder's and his pupils' cave. On the other side of the river, above, in a vineyard, Shammai and his wife are buried. Nearby is another cave, in which R' Binyamin bar Yefet is buried, and beside him R' Yose Hatifa. Near him is Yose ben Kisma's grave. In Benjamin’s Travels, he writes that R. Yehudah b. B. was also buried there [Adler’s edition reads Yehudah ben Bethera].

6. A distinguished pupil of R' Akiva. His face became discolored because R' Meir sat at the head. He told him, “It suffices you that I and your Creator recognize your power”: Jerusalem Sanhedrin, first chapter. In Menahot 72a: R' Elazar son of R' Shimon stated it in the approach of R' Akiva, his father's teacher. In Zevahim: R' Shimon stated it in the approach of R' Akiva, his teacher. ד״ק [provisionally: examine carefully]. In R' Akiva's name: Berakhot 8b. In Arvei Pesahim, he told R' Akiva while the latter was in prison, “If you do not teach me Torah, I shall tell my father Yohai, and he will hand you over to the government.” R' Akiva called him “my son”: Me'ilah 7a. In Tosefta Ohalot, chapter 4, and Kohen Gadol in Nazir 52b: because he said of R' Akiva that he did not retract until he died—whether he retracted after dying, he did not know—his teeth blackened from fasting, because it is improper conduct to speak thus of one's teacher. In Gittin, Ha-Tikabbel, 67a, he told his pupils, “Learn my teachings, for they are selections from the selections of R' Akiva's teachings.” [R. Shimon] would grind much and forget little. What he sifted out was only bran. He was also a pupil in the days of R' Yehoshua and Rabban Gamliel, when he asked whether the evening prayer is optional or obligatory: Tefillat ha-Shahar, 27b. He studied with R' Yohanan ben Nuri: Eruvin, first chapter; see his entry, where he was his colleague. He was ordained by R' Yehudah ben Bava; see his entry. He was Rabbi's teacher. In his days monetary judgments ceased from Israel: Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Arba Mitot.

7. Sefer Keritut, Yemot Olam, gate 3, writes: R' Meir and R' Shimon—the halakhah follows the stricter one. The halakhah follows R' Shimon on Shabbat, but concerning muktzeh arising from a Torah prohibition it does not follow R' Shimon. Responsa Havvot Ya'ir writes that R' Meir versus R' Shimon remains unresolved. R' Shmuel ha-Nagid's Mevo ha-Gemara says that the halakhah follows R' Shimon; so too it appears in Asheri, end of Avodah Zarah, chapter 2, no. 34, and in the introduction to Etz Hayyim's commentary, that this is what Jerusalem Demai, chapter 5, says. See also what I wrote at the end of Hullin, chapter 9. The statement about R' Meir in Eruvin, “Why did they not establish the halakhah according to him?” [chapter 9 in this witness, parallel at 13b in chapter 1] also implies against everyone who disagrees with him; see Tosafot Yom Tov, Hullin, chapter 9. In the future the halakhah will follow R' Shimon ben Yohai; see above, Shammai. See Tosafot, Shabbat 110b: the halakhah follows R' Shimon that an unintended act is permitted throughout the Torah.

Concerning a defect in the altar, Rambam rules in accordance with R' Shimon ben Yohai, not R' Eliezer ben Yaakov. Kesef Mishneh writes that this is because R' Shimon ben Yohai was more a master of Talmud than R' Eliezer ben Yaakov. See responsa Hakham Tzevi, no. 10: a sage asked that Kesef Mishneh had overlooked the Gemara in Menahot, “And the first fruits follow R' Eliezer ben Yaakov.” Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explains, “Because his stature is great.” This implies that the halakhah follows him against R' Yehudah, and all the more against R' Shimon, since we hold that R' Yehudah versus R' Shimon—the halakhah follows R' Yehudah. End of the questioner's words. He answered that this is no objection: Kesef Mishneh too agrees that the halakhah follows him in the Mishnah against anyone, and there it is a mishnah. The statement that R' Shimon ben Yohai is a master of Talmud means: since it is taught in the Mishnah, the halakhah follows him; that is why the Mishnah cites him in preference to R' Yehudah. It is true that even in the Mishnah Rambam ruled like R' Akiva, not R' Eliezer ben Yaakov, concerning the measurement for the beheaded calf; see his entry. But R' Shimon ben Yohai told his pupils that his teachings were selections from R' Akiva's teachings. End of quotation. Thus where one of R' Shimon ben Yohai's colleagues, such as R' Yehudah or R' Yose, who were also R' Akiva's pupils, did not disagree with him, one may say that the halakhah follows him against R' Eliezer ben Yaakov, because R' Shimon ben Yohai's words are surely the very words of his teacher R' Akiva, whom the halakhah follows against R' Eliezer ben Yaakov. But why specifically R' Eliezer ben Yaakov in a baraita—even in the Mishnah too? Moreover, R' Eliezer ben Yaakov too was R' Akiva's pupil. Regarding the statement that R' Shimon ben Yohai was more a master of Talmud than R' Eliezer ben Yaakov, whose teaching was “a kav and clean,” Rashi explains: he did not learn as much as his colleagues [Rashi: he did not teach as much].

8. Ahiyah the Shilonite was reincarnated in R' Shimon ben Yohai to atone for the sin of signing for Yarovam to worship idols. Therefore R' Shimon ben Yohai said, “I can save the whole world until now; if Ahiyah joins me, until the end of all generations.” Hence he suffered in the cave to atone for all Israel: I Kings, chapter 12. See above, R' Elazar son of R' Shimon, for the reason he suffered thirteen years in the cave. R' Shimon ben Yohai is Yotam son of Uzziyah, and so forth, because R' Shimon ben Yohai is of the attribute of kindness, as appears from Ba-Meh Madlikin: on leaving the cave, wherever R' Elazar struck, R' Shimon ben Yohai healed. But according to what Tosafot write, that he was irascible and exacting over a small matter, it appears that he was of the attribute of judgment. In Bava Metzia, Ha-Po'alim, when suffering came upon R' Elazar he said, “Come, my brothers,” because he was of the attribute of judgment. This is what he said: “Were Elazar my son with me,” for he is judgment, and judgment and mercy do not settle together. For my merit alone is judgment; “I can exempt … from the day I was created; were Elazar my son with me”—R' Elazar was together with him—“from the day I was created until now; and Yotam with us,” because R' Shimon ben Yohai was of his spark and he was pious, but had a sin: “Only the high places were not removed.” Were it not for this, “I could … from the day the world was created and forever”: Gilgulei Neshamot. See Hesed le-Avraham, spring 5, river 25. In Emek ha-Melekh, 63a: R' Shimon ben Yohai corresponds to Moshe, but not in the mystery of Moshe's first supernal radiance, only in the aspect of the soul he had with the second tablets. At first R' Shimon ben Yohai was lower; afterward he rose to Moshe's rank; see there.

At the end of the introduction to Zohar printed in Sulzbach it writes: know that R' Shimon ben Yohai contained a spark of Moshe, and his generation corresponded to the generation of knowledge. Therefore he began Zohar with the word BeRiSh (ברי״ש), the initials of R' Shimon ben Yohai. Therefore he merited to see the stature of the wilderness generation, as mentioned in Zohar, Lekh Lekha, and so forth. Therefore he made Sifra di-Tzeni'uta in five chapters, corresponding to the five books of the Torah. Therefore he fled from the emperor, who said, “Shimon, who disparaged, shall be killed,” in the foregoing Ba-Meh Madlikin, just as Moshe fled Pharaoh and attained his perfection there in the wilderness. Likewise R' Shimon ben Yohai attained his perfection in the cave in the wilderness at Lod, for there God was revealed to him. End of quotation. In Kol Yaakov: Kayin's soul was not fully perfected in Yitro. After Yitro it came into R' Shimon ben Yohai for its repair—that is, he heard from Eliyahu. It brings proof from Targum Yonatan, Kedoshim: R' Elazar said, “Holy lamp … to kiss his hands,” and so forth.

9. Avtolmos was in his time. R' Avin reports in his name. Abba Elazar ben Doglai was in his time. And R' Eliezer ben Yaakov: Parah 9:2. R' Elazar son of R' Yose ben Halafta: see above. R' Dostai ben Yehudah reports in his name. Huna bar Bizna reports in his name. Rav Zutra reports in his name. R' Hanina reports in his name. Hananyah ben Hakhinai was his colleague. R' Hananyah ben Akashya. R' Yehudah ben Bava ordained him. R' Yehudah bar Illai disagrees with him. R' Yehudah ben Gerim: see above. R' Yehudah the Nasi was his pupil. And R' Yehoshua ben Korhah: Avodah Zarah 7, beginning of side b. R' Yehoshua ben Levi reports in his name. R' Yohanan the Sandal-maker asked him. R' Yohanan reports in his name. R' Yonatan ben Lakunya was in his time. R' Yose was his colleague. And R' Yannai. R' Yitzhak bar Bisna reports in his name. R' Yirmeyah reports in his name. In R' Levi Sukhya's or the Elder's name—requires examination. R' Mattyah ben Harash asked him. Nehorai bar Shanya reports in his name. And R' Nehemyah. Ulla Bira'ah reports in his name. R' Akiva was his teacher; see above. R' Pinhas ben Yair was his father-in-law. R' Reuven Itztrobuli was in his time. Rabbah reports in his name. R' Shaul of Naveh reports in his name. R' Shimon Shezuri was his colleague. R' Shimon ben Menasya disagrees with him. R' Shimon ben Yehudah of Kefar Akko reports in his name. R' Shimon ben Elazar reports in his name. R' Shimon bar Abba reports in his name.
